markdown.headingText: What Does a Pixel Mean Without Its Neighbours?
markdown.markdown:
A satellite image is a matrix of numbers. Pick any pixel — say, position
$(100, 100)$. Its value is $142$. What does that mean?

Any digital image is just a matrix of numbers. Consider a satellite image of a region. Pick any pixel- say, position $(100, 100)$. Its value is $142$. What does it mean? Is it a road? A river? A rooftop? 

You cannot tell from a single number. The pixel at $(100, 100)$ only means something in relation to its
neighbours — $(99, 100)$, $(101, 100)$, $(100, 99)$. The number $142$ is
not information. The *relationship* between $142$ and its neighbours —
that is information.


![A satellite image — the pixel at (100,100) is marked. Without context, 
it means nothing.](images/satellite_image.png)

This is not just a quirk of satellite imagery. It is true for any kind of image. A single pixel value, say, a patch of skin tone near your cheek alone tells you nothing. What tells you something is the *neighborhood*- the eye above it, the jaw below it and the ear to its side. The pixel derives its meaning from what surrounds it. 


Now zoom out. This is not even specific to images. A word in a sentence 
works the same way. "Bank" means something completely different depending 
on whether its neighbours are "river" and "fish" or "loan" and "interest 
rate." But we will not go there — this book stays in vision, and images 
are already rich enough to make the point.

![The same pixel value appearing in two completely different contexts — 
once on a road, once on a river. Same number, different meaning.](images/pixel_context.png)

So here is the question this post is really asking:

> **How do we build a representation of a patch of an image that is 
> informed by all the other patches?**

Not a fixed representation. But something that is *context-dependent*- one that changes based on the neighborhood, the way a pixel's meaning changes based on what surrounds it. 

This is what attention does. And it turns out the path to attention runs 
through a surprisingly classical idea — the notion of **similarity** 
between vectors, and specifically, what it means to measure similarity 
*well*.

But before we get to the math, let us set the scene properly.

## Setting the Scene

Suppose we have an image. We divide it into a grid of non-overlapping 
patches — say, $16 \times 16$ pixel blocks. Each patch is flattened into 
a vector. For a colour image with 3 channels, a $16 \times 16$ patch 
gives a vector of $16 \times 16 \times 3 = 768$ numbers.

![An image divided into a grid of patches. Each patch becomes a vector. 
The grid here is $16 \times 16$, giving 196 patches total.](images/patch_grid.png)

We now have a set of $N$ vectors:

$$\{\vec{x}_1, \vec{x}_2, \ldots, \vec{x}_N\}, \quad \vec{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^D$$

Think of each $\vec{x}_i$ as one patch. $N$ is the number of patches. 
$D$ is the dimension of each patch vector — $768$ in the example above.

We can stack these into a matrix:

$$X = \begin{bmatrix} — & \vec{x}_1^T & — \\ — & \vec{x}_2^T & — \\ 
& \vdots & \\ — & \vec{x}_N^T & — \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}$$

Each row is one patch. $X$ is our data matrix — $N$ patches, each with 
$D$ features.

Now, the raw patch vectors $\vec{x}_i$ are just pixel values — low-level 
information. They have no awareness of the rest of the image. Patch 47 
does not know what patch 48 looks like, or patch 12, or patch 196.

What we want is a new set of vectors:

$$\{\vec{y}_1, \vec{y}_2, \ldots, \vec{y}_N\}, \quad \vec{y}_i \in \mathbb{R}^D$$

where $\vec{y}_n$ is a *richer* version of $\vec{x}_n$ — one that has 
looked around at the other patches and incorporated relevant information 
from them. The output matrix:

$$Y = \begin{bmatrix} — & \vec{y}_1^T & — \\ — & \vec{y}_2^T & — \\ 
& \vdots & \\ — & \vec{y}_N^T & — \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}$$

has the same shape as $X$. Same number of patches, same dimension. But 
the representations are no longer context-free — each $\vec{y}_n$ has 
been informed by the whole image.

![Input patches $X$ on the left — each patch is isolated. Output 
representations $Y$ on the right — each patch now carries information 
from the others. The arrows suggest which patches informed which.](images/attention_intuition.png)

This transformation — from $X$ to $Y$, from isolated patches to 
context-aware representations — is what a transformer layer does. 

The question is how. And the answer starts with a deceptively simple 
idea: **weighted averaging**.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
A transformer does not obtain context from nowhere. It computes 
$\vec{y}_n$ as a weighted sum of all the input vectors 
$\vec{x}_1, \ldots, \vec{x}_N$. The weights determine how much each 
patch contributes to the representation of patch $n$. Computing those 
weights intelligently — that is the attention mechanism.
:::

In the next section, we ask: what should those weights look like? And 
that question leads us directly to the mathematics of similarity.
